_comment: Hand-resolved control flow the static trace cannot follow on its own, fed back into tools/trace-code.py as extra knowledge. An empty 'unresolved' list would be a WEAKER statement than it sounds - it would say every table this file knows about is resolved, not that every table is in the file. A gap whose first bytes are a run of plausible addresses is a table nobody registered.
_inline_calls_comment: Routines called with their argument written inline after the JSR. Each pops its own return address and reads forward from it, so the bytes following the call are DATA and a trace that decodes them is guaranteed to produce nonsense that still looks like instructions. This list is the result of enumerating the mechanism class rather than chasing the sites: a scan for PLA/STA $zp/PLA/STA $zp+1 - a routine taking its own return address as a pointer - finds eleven matches in the ROM, of which five are byte-scan false positives inside data and six are real. Registered here with a 'kind' that says how many bytes follow and whether control ever comes back.

inline_calls.name: queue inline PPU string (address inline)
inline_calls.description: CORRECTION. This was registered as a variable-length stream whose termination could not be established, on the reading that $D57C-$D584 loops over a run of items. It does not. It loops over ONE item, waiting for room: $D7C3 never touches $16/$17, so re-entering $D591 re-tests the same bytes. Exactly one item is consumed per call and the block length is a function of its first byte. What the loop is really doing: $D591 computes the item's length and hands it to $D6C0, which adds it to $21 - the fill level of a PPU write queue staged at $0100 - and clears carry only when the item fits. Carry set means no room, so $D7C3 is called to drain the queue and the same item is tested again. The thresholds are the queue's: $51 is the hard limit, $31 an early-flush point taken when $A5 is non-zero. $D587 then copies the item in through $D5A5 and advances $16 past exactly its own bytes, and $D58A pushes the advanced pointer back so the caller resumes after the block. FORMAT: [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters], so the block is count + 3 bytes. The length rule read off $D591 is (first byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0 and 9 at or above, and $D5A5 advances $16 by exactly that. CONFIRMED AT EVERY SITE: all 20 call sites of this routine and of $D53F resume on a legal opcode under this rule, and 16 of the 20 payloads read as English - GAME OVER, CONGRATULATIONS, YOU GOT ITEM, SOUND TEST, GO OUT, WRONG WORD, THE ABOVE, WORD IS RIGHT, AREA, YOUR FINAL SCORE. Characters are ASCII for A-Z and space. CORRECTION: an earlier version of this entry said no site in the ROM uses a count in $80-$BF and that bit 7 therefore had no example to read. That was written before the trace reached bank 0 $845F and $8469, which both call this routine with a count of $83 - three characters, six bytes, exactly as the (byte & $7F) + 3 rule says. So bit 7 IS used. What it MEANS is still not established: it is masked off before the length is computed, but the count byte is copied into the queue whole, so the queue's consumer at $D7C3 and beyond sees it. Both sites write to PPU $2286 and differ only in where the ':' sits among two spaces.

inline_calls.name: queue inline PPU string (address from $18/$19)
inline_calls.description: The same mechanism as $D576 and the same length rule, with one difference that changes the block size: **the PPU address is not in the stream.** $D550-$D56F writes the count byte, then $19 and $18 from RAM, into the queue header, and only then copies characters - and it sets $11 to length MINUS 3 rather than length. So the block is [count][count characters], count + 1 bytes, two fewer than $D576's. Worked example, bank 7 $F5CC: 0C then ' YOU GOT KEY' - twelve characters, thirteen bytes, resuming at $F5D9 on LDY #$28 / JSR $FF8B. The two - 2 is not a guess: $D558 is SEC / SBC #$03 and the copy resumes at $D5AF with Y already advanced by one more than $D5A5 leaves it.

inline_calls.name: four-byte inline argument
inline_calls.description: The one member of this class whose inline length is a constant, and therefore the one the trace can step over instead of stopping at. It pops its return address into $16/$17, reads exactly four bytes through ($16),Y with Y running 1 to 4 into $15, $19, $18 and $14, calls $D5F8, then adds 4 to $16 and reaches $D58A, which pushes the advanced pointer and RTSes. Four is read off the ADC #$04 at $D5EC and confirmed by the four LDA ($16),Y reads before it - two independent statements of the same number in the same routine. What the four bytes MEAN is not established; $15, $19, $18 and $14 have no RAM map yet.

inline_calls.name: inline jump table, indexed by Y
inline_calls.description: Not an argument but a dispatch. It pops its return address into $00/$01, does INY twice - Y arrives from the caller and is NOT initialised here, which is what makes it a table rather than a single address - then pushes the bytes at ($00),Y and ($00),Y-1 and RTSes into them. Because JSR pushed return-1 and RTS adds one back, entry k of the table is the two little-endian bytes at ret+2k holding target-1, and the caller selects it by arriving with Y = 2k. Control never comes back to the call site. The trace resolves the target when it knows Y and records a lead when it does not; either way it stops, because there is no resumption point. NOT ESTABLISHED: the entry count at any site. Nothing in the routine bounds Y, so the count has to come from the caller - per playbook section 3, from an index mask or a CPY bound, never from dividing the gap. This is the entry point for a caller that already holds Y = 2 x index; the ASL A / TAY two bytes earlier is the other entry point, registered separately, for a caller holding the index in A.

inline_calls.name: inline jump table, indexed by Y (bank 5 copy)
inline_calls.description: Byte-identical to $D6B0 and to the bank 6 copy at $85F6: eleven bytes, PLA/STA $00/PLA/STA $01/INY/INY/LDA ($00),Y/PHA/DEY/LDA ($00),Y/PHA/RTS. Three banks each carrying their own copy of the same helper is the idiom playbook section 5 names - several banks each carry their own decompressor rather than sharing one - and it is worth knowing here because a bank can dispatch this way without ever calling into bank 7. This is the entry point for a caller that already holds Y = 2 x index; the ASL A / TAY two bytes earlier is the other entry point, registered separately, for a caller holding the index in A.

inline_calls.name: inline jump table, indexed by Y (bank 6 copy)
inline_calls.description: Byte-identical to $D6B0 and to the bank 5 copy at $9F12. See those entries. This is the entry point for a caller that already holds Y = 2 x index; the ASL A / TAY two bytes earlier is the other entry point, registered separately, for a caller holding the index in A.

inline_calls.name: inline jump table, indexed by A (doubling entry to $D6B0)
inline_calls.description: Two bytes - ASL A / TAY - falling straight through into $D6B0. Same mechanism, different calling convention: the caller passes the entry number in A and this doubles it into the byte offset Y that the body wants. Found because the trace derailed at call sites of THIS address while the body two bytes later was already registered, which is the shape playbook section 5 calls a handler that presets one byte and falls into its neighbour: two entries a few bytes apart are one routine, not two. Worked example, bank 7 $E6F0: JSR $D6AE followed by ten little-endian words 06 E7, 20 E7, 32 E7, 5F E7, 89 E7, 9E E7, B5 E7, 5D E8, 80 E8, 92 E8 - all of them $E7xx/$E8xx, i.e. addresses just past the call site, which is what a local dispatch table looks like. NOT ESTABLISHED: the entry count. Ten is where the plausible addresses stop at that one site and is not a claim about any other.

_rejected_comment: Matches of the PLA/STA $zp/PLA/STA $zp+1 scan that are NOT inline-argument calls, written down so the next reader does not re-derive them. Recording the rejects is what makes the class enumeration a finding rather than a list.

rejected.why: The bytes decode to PLA/STA $18/PLA/STA $19/BCC $8136/BRK. A BRK two instructions in says this is not an instruction boundary; the match is a byte-scan false positive inside data.
Real code, but it pops FOUR bytes - two return addresses - into $18/$19 and $14/$15 and then uses them as values, not as a pointer to inline data. Nothing reads through ($18) or ($14) here.
The second half of the $810C sequence, matched separately by the scan. Not a routine head.

Pops its return address into $18/$19 and immediately RTSes - so it returns to its caller's caller, having left its own return address in RAM as a value. A 'where was I called from' helper, not an inline-argument call.

Pops its return address into $18/$19, then treats the two bytes as a coordinate pair - AND #$F0, LSR, five more LSRs, ORA - and indexes with the result. It reads the address, not the bytes the address points at.

unresolved: $8A97 in bank 2: JMP ($10C0). $10C0 mirrors to $00C0 in the 2 KB of CPU RAM, so this is a jump through a RAM vector - the mechanism playbook section 4 records as hiding a quarter of a bank on another cartridge. Nothing that installs it has been looked for yet.

Bank 4 is reached at 19 bytes of 16,384. Its opening JMP table has a single entry, which is the odd one out among the eight banks, and no far call in the ROM targets it. Whatever reaches bank 4 is a mechanism nothing here has enumerated.
What bit 7 of a PPU-string count byte means. Two sites use it, bank 0 $845F and $8469, both writing to PPU $2286.
What the $C0-and-above form of a PPU-string item is. Two sites use it, bank 5 $86DD and $86EE, and its length is the fixed 9 rather than a character count. Its payload is not ASCII.
Every call site of the three jump_table helpers: the inline table's entry count is not established at any of them, so none of their targets beyond the one the index selects is reached.
_ppu_string_comment: The PPU write queue these two feed: $0100 is the buffer, $21 its fill level, $20 a count of entries, $25 the length of the entry being added, $24 scratch. $D6E0 opens an entry and returns the write position in A; $D6F7 commits it. $D7C3 drains. None of that is claimed as understood beyond what these two routines need.

character_encoding.summary: Plain ASCII for A-Z, 0-9, space and ':', with at least five extra glyphs at $5B-$5F.
character_encoding.evidence: Sixteen of the 32 text blocks read as English on a straight ASCII reading with no substitutions - GAME OVER, CONGRATULATIONS, CONTINUE PUSH START, GO TO THE NEXT SPACE, YOU GOT ITEM, SOUND TEST, WORD CHECK, WRONG WORD, GO OUT, CHIP MAX, WEAPON POWER, USE CHIP, ATTACK, SHIELD, AREA, YOUR FINAL SCORE, YOU GOT KEY. That many independent blocks agreeing is not a coincidence that needs arguing about. Across every text payload the only codes outside A-Z and space are $30, $33, $3A, $5B, $5C, $5D, $5E and $5F, and the first three are '0', '3' and ':' in ASCII, which fit their contexts ('0  CHIP', '3', ':  ').
character_encoding.glyphs_5C_5F: $5C-$5F are graphics, not letters, and the layout says so rather than the shapes. Bank 1 $811C writes $5C $5E to PPU $21AF and bank 1 $8124 writes $5D $5F to PPU $21CF. Those two addresses are 32 bytes apart, which is one nametable row, so the four tiles form a 2x2 block - a single symbol two tiles wide and two tall. No guess about what it depicts.
character_encoding.glyph_5B: LEAD, not established. $5B sits immediately after 'Z' ($5A) and appears three times: at the end of 'CONGRATULATIONS' and twice in 'FR[ BA[ END'. A full stop fits all three readings - 'CONGRATULATIONS.', 'FR. BA. END' - and nothing else obvious does. That is resemblance, which per playbook section 10 is a lead and never a confirmation, and the thing that would settle it is the font. There is no font to look at: CHR is RAM on this cartridge and no uploader has been found, so the tiles do not exist anywhere in this file as tiles. Re-check this entry when one turns up.
